Female rock sole attain a maximum total length of 60 cm [Li = 60 cm], a value that notably exceeds the 58 cm [Li = 58 cm] recorded for males, reflecting a pattern of sexual size dimorphism common among pleuronectids. The length at which females first achieve puberty has been determined to be 34.7 cm [Lp = 34.7 cm], based on macroscopic examination of gonadal development in specimens collected from the Gulf of Alaska. This size threshold corresponds closely with a wet weight at puberty of 488 g [Wwp = 488 g], derived from the length-weight relationship established for this population. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight for females, representing the asymptotic body mass approached by large adults, is estimated at 2600 g [Wwi = 2600 g], a figure that underscores the substantial increase in somatic mass between maturation and full adulthood. Field surveys indicate that these life-history parameters are shaped by the cold, productive waters of the North Pacific, where growth rates are moderate but sustained over many years.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was 18% [GSI = 18%] when measured at a water temperature of 4.7 °C [T = 4.7 °C]. This index, calculated as the ratio of ovary mass to somatic mass, provides a direct measure of the energetic allocation toward gamete production during the prespawning period. The thermal regime at which these measurements were obtained is typical of the species' benthic habitat during the late winter spawning season, when adults aggregate on soft bottoms at depths between 50 and 150 meters.

The initial wet weight of newly hatched rock sole larvae is remarkably low at 0.0004 grams [Wwb = 0.0004 grams], a mass that corresponds to the small oil-globule diameter of approximately 0.92 mm observed in the pelagic eggs. This minute birth mass places the species among the smallest pleuronectid larvae at the onset of exogenous feeding, necessitating a highly efficient yolk-sac utilization period. The lecithotrophic larva must complete yolk absorption within the first few days post-hatch before the mouth opens and active prey capture begins. Trophic transition occurs when the larva reaches roughly 3 to 4 mm in standard length, at which point the finfold begins to differentiate and the gut becomes fully functional. The protracted pelagic larval phase, lasting several weeks to months depending on temperature, exposes these tiny individuals to substantial advection by prevailing currents, which influences both settlement success and the geographic extent of population connectivity across the species' range.

Maximum documented lifespan in wild rock sole populations reaches approximately 26 years [am = approximately 26 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of the Bering Sea, where bottom temperatures average approximately 5.1 °C [T = 5.1 °C]. This longevity is among the highest recorded for the Pleuronectidae and reflects the slow somatic growth and delayed reproductive maturation characteristic of this cold-water species. Otolith-based age estimates from long-term fishery-independent surveys confirm that individuals beyond 20 years of age are regularly encountered, though the majority of the spawning biomass is composed of fish between 8 and 15 years old. The extended lifespan allows rock sole to buffer against years of poor recruitment by maintaining multiple reproductive opportunities across decades, a classic bet-hedging strategy in variable marine environments. Senescence in very old individuals is inferred from declining condition factors and reduced fecundity, though precise mechanistic data on age-related physiological deterioration in this species remain limited.

Settlement from the pelagic larval stage to the benthic juvenile habitat represents a critical transition in the life cycle of rock sole. Recently metamorphosed juveniles recruit to shallow nearshore nurseries where they begin feeding on small infaunal invertebrates. Growth during the first year is rapid, with individuals often exceeding 10 cm by the end of their first winter. The length-weight relationship used to predict mass from length, expressed as 0.00912 multiplied by length raised to the 3.07 power, was developed from a large sample of specimens collected across the species' geographic range and provides a robust tool for estimating body condition. This allometric coefficient, slightly above 3, indicates that rock sole exhibit a mildly positive allometric growth pattern, meaning larger individuals are proportionally heavier than a strict isometric relationship would predict. Such growth characteristics are typical of flatfishes that accumulate substantial lipid reserves in the liver and muscle tissue as a buffer against seasonal food scarcity.
